Magnetostratigraphic study of a Late Cretaceous–Paleogene succession
in the eastern Xining basin, NE Tibet: Constraint on the timing of
major tectonic events in response to the India-Eurasia collision

2 School of Earth and Space Sciences, Peking University, Beijing 100871, China
3 School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210023, China

The Xining basin in the NE margin of the Cretaceous red beds are divided into two posits (QBGMR, 1991; Dai et al., 2006; Fang
Tibetan Plateau (Fig. 1) provides an optimal groups separated by an unconformity. The et al., 2019) (Fig. 2), which unconformably
environment for unraveling such significant far-
field effects. Tectonism triggered by the distant
plate collision and subsequent incision by the
Huangshui River and its tributaries exposed the
Cretaceous to Neogene sequences with numer-
ous index fossils, which have been investigated
by many authors (e.g., Horton et al., 2004; Dai
et al., 2006; Dupont-Nivet et al., 2007; Abels
et al., 2011; Hoorn et al., 2012; Xiao et al., 2010,
2012; Bosboom et al., 2014; Zan et al., 2015;
Sayem et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2019; Yang
et al., 2019).
Here we present the magnetostratigraphy
study of a Late Cretaceous to Paleogene suc-
cession of the Zhongba section outcropping in
the southern margin of the eastern Xining ba-
sin, in an attempt to determine the age of the
K-Pg unconformity and to explore its tectonic
significance. Detailed magnetostratigraphy was
conducted in combination with detrital zircon
provenance and anisotropy of magnetic sus-
ceptibility (AMS) analyses, which allow for the
establishment of a tectonic evolution history of
the Xining basin during the period of Late Cre-
taceous to early Cenozoic. The result offers new
insights into the early response in the NE Tibetan
margin to the transition from Neo-Tethys oce-
anic plate subduction to the India-Eurasia colli-
sion in southern Tibet and along the Himalayas.

STRATIGRAPHY

Figure 3. (A) Detailed geological map of the southern margin of the Xining basin and the northern Laji Shan frontal fault zone; (B–C)
The northern Laji Shan frontal fault which thrusts the pre-Cretaceous basement rocks northward over the Late Cretaceous Minhe
Group along its western segment; (D) The junction zone between the eastern and western segments of the frontal fault is a low-angle
detachment zone with fault breccia composed of pre-Cenozoic volcanic rocks, and overlain by Early Cretaceous conglomerates, they
together thrust northward over the Late Cretaceous Minhe Group; (E) A brief stratigraphic column of the Cretaceous–Paleogene suc-
cession in the southeastern Xining basin and two unconformities with this column. The lower one is between the Cretaceous strata and
Paleogene muddy sandstone unit, the upper one is within the Paleogene–Neogene successions.

Figure 17. Sketch showing deformation model of the Tibetan Plateau during Late Cretaceous 70–60 Ma (A) and Paleogene 55–22 Ma (B),
and the cross-section (C) displaying the plate tectonics and potential dynamics. Planar model (location and size of the Greater-Lesser
Himalaya and India with respect to Tibet) was adapted from Yuan et al. (2020) and Cao et al. (2021). 3-D model (cross-section) was re-
ferred to Tapponnier et al. (2001); Cowgill et al. (2003); and Conrad and Lithgow (2004). Names of the major crustal blocks and sutures
are shown. BNS—Bangong-Nujiang suture; JS—Jinsha suture; ATF—Altyn Tagh fault; TTS—Tanggula thrust system; QLTB—Qilian
thrust belt; CMB—Changma basin; LZ—Longzhong basin; LPB—Liupanshan basin; TRB—Tarim basin; QB—Qaidam basin; XNB—
Xining basin; HXB—Hoh Xil basin; GJB—Gonjo basin; YNB—Yushu-Nangqian basin; JCB—Jianchuan basin; LPB—Lanping basin;
MPT-WKTB—Main Pamir thrust–West Kunlun thrust belt; QNTB—North Qaidam thrust; CQLB—Central Qilian structural belt;
HYF—Haiyuan fault; LATB—Liupanshan arcuate tectonic belt; QT—Qaidam thrust; WQLT—West Qinling thrust; LMC—Lung-
muco fault; YNTB—Yushu-Nangqian thrust belt; GJT—Gonjo thrust; LZTB—Ludian-Zhonghejiang fold-and-thrust belt; SGAT—
Shiquanhe-Gaize-Amdo thrust; ALS-RRF—Ailaoshan-Red river fault; CS-LCJF—Chongshan-Lancangjiang fault; LMST—Longmen
Shan thrust belt. Initial timing for major faults is labeled: Altyn Tagh fault during the Cretaceous Period (Li and Yang, 2004; Arnaud
et al., 2003); East Qilian tectonic belt at ca. 85–68 Ma (Pan et al., 2013); Tanggula thrust system at ca. 71.9 Ma (Jin et al., 2018); Gonjo
thrust at ca. 54 Ma (Zhang et al., 2018); Himalayan fold-and-thrust belt at ca. 50–45 Ma (Guillot et al., 2003; DeCelles et al., 2014);
Lungmuco fault at 60–55 Ma (Leloup et al., 2012); Ludian-Zhonghejiang fold-and-thrust belt at ca. 50 Ma (Cao et al., 2021); Main
Pamir thrust-West Kunlun thrust belt at ca. 50 Ma (Cao et al., 2013, 2015; Yin et al., 2002); North Qaidam thrust at 65–50 Ma (Yin et al.,
2008a); Qaidam thrust and Main Altyn Tagh fault at ca. 49 Ma (Yin et al., 2002); Shiquanhe-Gaize-Amdo thrust at <42.5 Ma (Yin and
Harrison, 2000); West Qinling thrust at ca. 50 Ma (Clark et al., 2010; Duvall et al., 2011); and Yushu-Nangqian thrust belt at ca. 51 Ma
(Horton et al., 2002; Spurlin et al., 2005); Central Qilian tectonic belt earlier than ca. 33 Ma (Yin et al., 2002); Central Kunlun tectonic
belt at ca. 35 Ma (Clark et al., 2010); Longmen Shan thrust belt at ca. 30 Ma (Wang et al., 2012a); Chongshan-Lancangjiang fault at ca.
32 Ma (Zhang et al., 2010a).
